Esther Reed, who allegedly leveraged the missing woman's identity to secure college admission, was taken into custody by U.S. Marshals. After evading capture for more than a year, Reed was arrested Saturday in suburban Chicago, according to Clark Brazier, a spokesman for the police department in Travelers Rest, South Carolina. She is scheduled to appear at a bond hearing in Illinois this week, while South Carolina authorities pursue her extradition on charges of aggravated identity theft and wire fraud.

Investigators report that Reed assumed the identity of Brooke Henson, who was 20 years old when she vanished from Travelers Rest more than eight years ago. # High School Dropout Nabbed After Stealing Identity to Enroll at Elite Universities

(CNN) -- Authorities announced Sunday the capture of a woman who never finished high school but managed to infiltrate two prestigious Ivy League institutions by assuming the stolen identity of a South Carolina woman who vanished years earlier.

Following more than twelve months on the run, Esther Reed was taken into custody Saturday in the Chicago suburbs by federal marshals, according to Clark Brazier, who serves as spokesperson for the Traveler's Rest, South Carolina police force. This week, Reed will face a bond hearing in Illinois, while South Carolina officials work to have her extradited on wire fraud and aggravated identity theft charges.

Investigators say Reed adopted the persona of Brooke Henson, a woman who went missing at age 20 more than eight years prior, vanishing from Travelers Rest without explanation. According to Jon Campbell, an investigator with the Travelers Rest Police Department who previously spoke with CNN, the method by which Reed acquired Henson's personal details remains murky—but she leveraged this stolen identity to sit for the SAT and GED exams before submitting college applications under Henson's name.

Both Harvard and Columbia have confirmed that someone named Brooke Henson was indeed a student at their institutions, though privacy regulations prevent them from elaborating further.

Brooke's aunt, Lisa Henson, shared mixed emotions with CNN on Sunday: "There's a bit of relief that comes with this news. But Brooke remains missing. I want answers. I'd give anything to confront her face-to-face and tell her exactly what a despicable human being she is."

Investigators maintain they don't believe Reed played any role in Henson's original disappearance. The prevailing theory among authorities is that someone in Henson's circle of acquaintances was responsible for her presumed death—yet without a recovered body, no arrests have followed.

For years, the Henson family remained in the dark about their loved one's fate—until summer 2006 brought what seemed like miraculous news. New York City officials contacted Travelers Rest police claiming Henson had been located safe in Manhattan, and this information was passed along to her relatives.

"I was overjoyed, just jumping around," Lisa Henson recalled. "It felt unbelievable." That elation crumbled, however, once it emerged the woman in New York wasn't Henson at all—it was Reed in disguise.

A former romantic partner revealed to CNN that Reed, while impersonating Henson, frequently boasted of making her living as a professional chess competitor with world-class skill. He admitted he took her claims at face value until he decided to test her by playing a match himself—and won.

Hailing from the small community of Townsend, Montana, Reed had actually been reported missing by her own family back in 1999—coincidentally around the same period Henson disappeared. Academic records from her Montana high school years show she struggled with poor grades. Her former English instructor, James Therriault, described her as easily overlooked: "Esther was the kind of kid who would have been invisible if you didn't take pains to notice her presence."

*CNN's Gary Tuchman and Ashley Fantz contributed to this report.*
